tomb_guide.text: Quiet, please. This is a five-thousand-year-old burial chamber, not a bus shelter. I'll turn out the lights, and you'll see what the sun did every winter.
The lights go down, the lamp goes gold, a single beam crawls up the floor. People gasp. A few cry. I've seen a grown man ask for his mother.

then.text: Kerrigan stands in the passage, her briefcase open on a stone, her umbrella forgotten.

else.text: The passage at Newgrange. Five thousand years old, three metres of cold stone on either side, and a very modern woman with a briefcase in the middle of it.
The Wardstone goes here, right at the chamber mouth, to catch the very first light. I've told the Wardens it is exactly like installing a satellite dish.
Ah. You found your way past the barrier. I did say 'private event'. I put it in writing. Twice. In green.
Five thousand years this tomb has waited for the sunrise. And now it has a sponsor.
Step aside. The light comes in at dawn and the Wardstone will catch it. And whatever comes with it.
Outside, a thin line of gold crosses the Boyne. Inside, the tomb lamp is gone. The passage is as dark as the inside of a closed fist.
A single beam of winter sunrise slides in through the roof-box above the door and crawls up the floor of the passage, slow as honey.
There. It's working. It's actually working. The Wardstone's picking up the light. Look at the readout. It's all lines. It's lovely.
The light climbs the carved spirals on the stones. The spirals begin to move. They aren't spirals. They are wings.
A figure unfolds out of the stone: tall, long-haired, wrapped in feathers like a cloak. A crow on each shoulder, a third on the lintel. Three voices speak as one.
Cé a chuir an fál seo anseo? Who put this fence here?
Siobhán Kerrigan, Regional Director. It's a, er, heritage project. Stakeholder engagement. Terms and conditions apply, in, um, the appendix.
Bhí an talamh anseo romhat. The land was here before you. I have judged kings. I have judged armies. Once, a man with a clipboard. He was wrong, too.
A crow hops down, takes the grey Wardstone in its beak, and carries it out along the passage. Far away, very small, there is a splash.
The Enclosure is weighed, and found wanting. The fence is weighed, and found wanting. The booking system is weighed, and found mildly amusing. But wanting.
Kerrigan looks at the briefcase, at the crows, at the beam of light on the floor. Then, slowly, she lifts her lanyard over her head.
I think I'd like to hand in my lanyard. Is there someone I give it to? It's a deactivation protocol. It's on page fourteen.
The third crow takes the lanyard, barcode and all, and flies out into the dawn to build a very uncomfortable nest.
I came here on a school tour, you know. Nine years old. I wanted it to be mine so badly that I thought a laminator would do.
Go raibh maith agat, to both of you. For not letting me. I'll write my resignation by hand. On paper. I haven't done that in years.
She picks up her umbrella, nods once to the Morrígan, and walks out into the sunrise without a lanyard, a briefcase or a plan. She looks lighter.
Walker. I have watched you from the lintel since the first Stone. Seven times the land has told me your name.
I will not be bound. I will be met. Come to my chamber, if you would test yourself against the Morrígan.
End of Wildlore v0.3. The North is waiting.
You are free to keep exploring. The Morrígan is waiting in the inner chamber.

then.text: The inner chamber is quiet. A single black feather lies on the stone, still warm. Somewhere in the passage, a crow is laughing.

else.text: The inner chamber is cold and old. In the centre, a shape of feathers and shadow, with eyes like winter. Three crows watch from the roof.
You have come. Good. I do not give myself. I am met. Show me what a walker is.

then.text: The Morrígan steps out of the stone and falls in beside you, black wings folded, three crows circling once over your head. She has chosen to walk with a walker. It is, you suspect, the quietest and most terrifying honour in Ireland.

else.text: The Morrígan dissolves into a storm of crows that spirals up through the roof-box and away. The chamber goes quiet. She will wait, if you want to try again.
The inner chamber is cold and dark. A single crow sits on a stone, watching you. Nothing happens.

gate_tomb.text: Private event. Solstice. Ms Kerrigan has the whole tomb booked, and she's very particular about the guest list.
Don't look at me, I just hold the rope. The rope is the whole job.
